Based on these inputs, the secondary fuel controller determines an injection amount of the secondary fuel and controls the pump accordingly. The secondary controller may also implement an additional control strategy in which the determined injection amount of the secondary fuel is modified based on at least one of the topographical conditions of the roads on which the vehicle is traveling and considerations of efficient engine output relative to driver requests for engine output.
outputs.L2: A supplemental fuel delivery arrangement for a diesel internal combustion engine comprises an injector configured to introduce an oxygen-bearing auxiliary fuel into the engine air intake, a pump that supplies the auxiliary fuel to the injector, a pressure sensor for detecting pressure within the intake system, and an auxiliary fuel control unit. This controller receives signals from the pressure sensor and the pump, engine operator commands, and engine operating information supplied by the primary engine controller. Using these inputs, it calculates the quantity of auxiliary fuel to be injected and regulates the pump accordingly. The auxiliary controller may also perform an added control function in which the calculated auxiliary fuel injection quantity is adjusted according to one or more factors, including the road terrain over which the vehicle is moving and engine-efficiency considerations relative to the driver’s requested engine output.
outputs.L3:
A secondary fueling system for a diesel engine is configured to introduce an oxygen-containing secondary fuel into the engine’s air intake system. By supplying the secondary fuel through the intake air stream, the system can supplement the primary diesel fuel delivered by the engine’s main fuel system and support improved combustion under selected operating conditions.

The system includes a secondary fuel injector positioned to deliver the oxygen-containing fuel into the air intake system, a pump for supplying the secondary fuel to the injector, an air intake pressure sensor, and a secondary fuel controller. The air intake pressure sensor monitors pressure conditions within the intake system, while the pump provides the required fuel flow and pressure for injection.

The secondary fuel controller receives and processes multiple inputs to determine how and when the secondary fuel should be injected. These inputs may include signals from the air intake pressure sensor, operating feedback or status signals from the pump, operator inputs, and engine operating data from the main engine controller. The engine operating data may include information such as engine speed, load, fueling rate, boost pressure, torque demand, temperature conditions, or other parameters relevant to engine performance.

Based on these inputs, the secondary fuel controller determines an appropriate injection amount of the oxygen-containing secondary fuel. The controller then controls operation of the pump, and optionally the injector, so that the selected amount of secondary fuel is delivered to the air intake system. In this way, the secondary fueling system can coordinate secondary fuel delivery with current engine conditions and driver demand.

The injection amount may also be adjusted in response to road topology and vehicle operating conditions. For example, the controller may account for whether the vehicle is traveling uphill, downhill, or on level terrain, as well as anticipated changes in engine load. The controller may further evaluate efficient engine output relative to the driver’s requested power. When the driver’s power request can be met more efficiently with supplemental secondary fuel, the controller may increase the injection amount. Conversely, when secondary fueling would be less beneficial or unnecessary, the controller may reduce or suspend injection. This allows the system to provide secondary fuel in a manner that supports efficient engine operation while responding to both vehicle conditions and driver power demands.
outputs.L4:
A secondary fueling system for a diesel engine is configured to introduce an oxygen-containing auxiliary fuel into the engine’s intake air stream in a controlled manner. The system includes an auxiliary fuel supply, a pump for delivering the auxiliary fuel, an injector positioned to inject the auxiliary fuel into the air intake, an intake pressure sensor, and an electronic controller. During operation, the controller receives information from the intake pressure sensor and uses that information, together with signals associated with the auxiliary fuel pump, operator inputs, and data received from the main engine controller, to determine an appropriate quantity of auxiliary fuel to be delivered to the engine.

The auxiliary fuel may be an oxygenated fuel, such as an alcohol-based fuel or another combustible fuel containing oxygen, which can supplement the primary diesel fuel delivered through the engine’s conventional fuel system. By injecting the auxiliary fuel into the intake air, the system allows the fuel to mix with incoming air before combustion. This can promote more complete combustion, improve engine response, reduce certain emissions, and allow the engine to operate more efficiently under selected operating conditions.

The controller may calculate the desired secondary fuel injection amount based on a variety of real-time operating parameters. These may include intake manifold pressure, engine speed, engine load, throttle or accelerator position, fuel demand, boost pressure, pump operating status, and information supplied by the diesel engine’s primary electronic control unit. The controller may also monitor operator-selected settings, such as enable/disable commands, performance modes, economy modes, or other driver inputs that influence the amount of auxiliary fuel delivered.

In addition to responding to engine operating data, the system may adjust the secondary fuel injection strategy according to road or route conditions. For example, the controller may receive or calculate information relating to road topology, including grade, elevation changes, upcoming inclines, descents, or other terrain characteristics. When the vehicle approaches a hill or operates under increased load, the controller may increase, reduce, delay, or otherwise modify the auxiliary fuel delivery to match the anticipated engine demand. Conversely, during downhill travel, low-load operation, or conditions where auxiliary fueling would provide little benefit, the controller may reduce or suspend injection.

The system may also compare engine efficiency with driver demand to determine whether additional auxiliary fuel is beneficial. If the driver requests increased power but the engine is operating in a range where supplemental oxygenated fuel can improve combustion or efficiency, the controller may command a higher injection rate. If the driver demand is low, or if engine conditions indicate that auxiliary fueling would reduce efficiency or exceed desired operating limits, the controller may decrease the injected quantity or stop auxiliary fueling altogether.

By coordinating the secondary fueling system with sensor feedback, pump behavior, driver commands, engine controller data, route information, and efficiency calculations, the system provides more precise control over supplemental fuel delivery. This adaptive control allows the diesel engine to respond effectively to changing loads, terrain, and operating conditions. As a result, the system can improve fuel management, support better engine performance, enhance drivability, and potentially reduce emissions or fuel consumption compared with less responsive secondary fueling arrangements.

**The Power of “The”**

“The” is one of the smallest and most common words in the English language, yet it plays an important role in communication. It is a definite article, used to point to something specific. When we say “a book,” we may mean any book, but when we say “the book,” we refer to a particular one that the listener or reader can identify.

This simple word helps create clarity. It tells us that something is known, unique, or already mentioned. For example, “the sun” refers to the one sun we see in the sky, and “the teacher” may refer to a specific teacher in a classroom. Without “the,” many sentences would feel incomplete or less precise.

“The” is also powerful because it gives importance to a noun. Phrases like “the truth,” “the future,” and “the world” feel broad and meaningful. Although it is easy to overlook, “the” helps shape meaning in countless sentences every day.

In short, “the” may be a tiny word, but it has a big responsibility. It guides understanding, adds specificity, and makes language more exact.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a patent-style abstract for a secondary fueling system for a diesel engine that injects an oxygen-containing fuel into the air intake and uses pressure sensing, pump feedback, operator inputs, and main ECU data to control injection amount.
counterfactuals.output: A secondary fueling system for a diesel engine includes a reservoir containing an oxygen-containing supplemental fuel, an injection device positioned to introduce the supplemental fuel into an air intake of the engine, and a pump configured to deliver the supplemental fuel from the reservoir to the injection device. A controller is operatively coupled to a pressure sensor associated with the secondary fuel delivery path, to the pump for receiving pump operating feedback, to one or more operator input devices, and to a main engine electronic control unit for receiving engine operating data. The controller determines a desired supplemental fuel injection amount based on at least the sensed pressure, pump feedback, operator input, and engine operating data, and controls operation of the pump and/or injection device to meter the oxygen-containing fuel into intake air supplied to the diesel engine. The system thereby provides regulated secondary fueling responsive to engine conditions and user-selected operating parameters.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the invention of a diesel internal combustion engine secondary fuel controller that meters oxygenated supplemental fuel via an intake injector and adjusts delivery based on intake pressure, pump signals, engine controller data, and driver inputs.
counterfactuals.output:
The invention is a secondary fuel control system for diesel internal combustion engines that supplements normal diesel fueling with an oxygenated fuel delivered into the engine intake.

It uses an intake-mounted injector to meter the supplemental fuel, while a dedicated controller determines how much to deliver. The controller adjusts injection based on operating conditions such as intake manifold pressure or boost, signals related to the diesel fuel pump, data from the engine’s electronic controller, and driver inputs such as throttle demand or control settings.

By coordinating supplemental oxygenated fuel delivery with engine load and operating state, the system aims to improve combustion efficiency, power output, emissions performance, and/or fuel economy without replacing the primary diesel fuel system.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.output: A system for operating a diesel engine, comprising: a secondary-fuel reservoir containing an oxygen-containing fuel; an electrically controllable injector arranged to introduce the oxygen-containing fuel into an intake passage of the diesel engine; a pump configured to supply the oxygen-containing fuel from the reservoir to the injector; an intake-pressure sensor configured to generate a signal indicative of pressure in the intake passage; and a controller operatively coupled to the injector, the pump, and the intake-pressure sensor, the controller being configured to determine a desired delivery rate of the oxygen-containing fuel based at least in part on the intake-pressure signal, anticipated or measured road topology, engine operating conditions, and a comparison between fuel-efficiency optimization and driver-demanded output, and to command the pump and injector to deliver the oxygen-containing fuel to the intake passage in accordance with the desired delivery rate.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an abstract for an automotive patent involving a secondary fuel injection system for diesel engines where a separate controller determines supplemental fuel quantity from sensor signals, pump output, operator commands, and main engine controller data.
counterfactuals.output: A secondary fuel injection system for a diesel engine includes a supplemental fuel injector, a fuel supply and pump arrangement, and a secondary electronic controller separate from a main engine controller. The secondary controller receives signals representative of one or more engine operating conditions, pump output characteristics, operator commands, and data communicated from the main engine controller. Based on the received information, the secondary controller determines a supplemental fuel quantity to be delivered independently of, or in coordination with, a primary fuel injection system. The secondary controller actuates the supplemental injector to introduce the determined quantity of fuel into an intake, exhaust, combustion, or aftertreatment-related flow path to support functions such as power augmentation, emissions control, exhaust temperature management, regeneration, or engine operating optimization. The system permits supplemental fueling without requiring full control authority over the primary diesel fuel injection system.

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe, in patent language, a vehicle diesel engine supplemental fueling apparatus that injects oxygenated fuel into the air intake and modifies the injection amount according to road grade/topology and efficient engine output relative to driver requests.
counterfactuals.output:
A vehicle diesel engine supplemental fueling apparatus is provided for delivering an oxygenated supplemental fuel to an intake air stream of a compression-ignition engine and for varying the delivered quantity in accordance with operating conditions including road grade, route topology, and an efficient engine-output determination relative to a driver power request.

In one embodiment, the apparatus comprises a reservoir configured to contain an oxygenated fuel, such as an alcohol, ether, ester, oxygenated hydrocarbon blend, or other combustible fuel having chemically bound oxygen. A supply circuit fluidly connects the reservoir to at least one metering device positioned to introduce the oxygenated fuel into an intake passage of the diesel engine upstream of one or more cylinders. The metering device may comprise a solenoid injector, piezoelectric injector, atomizing nozzle, air-assisted nozzle, vaporizing element, or other controlled dosing device capable of dispensing a commanded mass or volume of the oxygenated fuel into the intake air flow.

A controller is operatively connected to the metering device and is configured to generate an injection command corresponding to a supplemental-fuel quantity. The controller receives one or more engine operating signals indicative of diesel-engine operation, including at least one of engine speed, engine load, boost pressure, intake manifold pressure, mass air flow, exhaust temperature, exhaust oxygen, fuel rail pressure, primary diesel injection quantity, accelerator pedal position, requested torque, actual torque, vehicle speed, transmission gear, and engine coolant temperature. The controller further receives or determines a vehicle route condition signal indicative of an upcoming or present road grade or topology. The route condition signal may be derived from a global navigation satellite system receiver, digital map data, elevation data, inertial measurement signals, accelerometer data, barometric pressure data, camera or radar road-profile data, vehicle-to-infrastructure data, or combinations thereof.

The controller includes, stores, or accesses an engine efficiency model or map defining an efficient output region for the diesel engine as a function of engine speed, load, torque, fuel consumption, brake-specific fuel consumption, emissions constraints, thermal limits, or combinations thereof. The controller compares a driver-requested output, such as a torque or power request derived from accelerator pedal position and vehicle operating state, with an efficient engine output determined from the efficiency model. Based at least in part on the comparison, the controller determines whether supplemental oxygenated-fuel injection will assist the engine in satisfying the driver request while maintaining or moving engine operation toward the efficient output region.

In operation, when the vehicle encounters or is predicted to encounter an uphill grade, increased load, acceleration demand, or other route topology requiring elevated engine output, the controller may increase the commanded supplemental oxygenated-fuel quantity if the driver-requested output exceeds or approaches the efficient diesel operating output and if engine and emissions conditions permit such injection. Conversely, when the vehicle is traveling on level terrain, downhill terrain, low-load conditions, deceleration conditions, or when the driver-requested output is at or below an efficient engine output threshold, the controller may reduce, inhibit, or discontinue supplemental oxygenated-fuel injection. The controller may also anticipatorily modify the injection amount based on upcoming road grade, for example by initiating or increasing supplemental fueling before a predicted climb, reducing supplemental fueling before a descent, or smoothing the injected quantity to prevent abrupt torque changes.

The supplemental fuel is preferably injected into the air intake in a finely atomized or vaporized form such that the oxygenated fuel mixes with the intake air before combustion. The introduced oxygenated fuel may supplement the primary diesel fuel charge delivered by the engine’s native diesel injection system, thereby providing additional combustible energy and oxygen-bearing constituents to the cylinder charge. The controller may coordinate the supplemental-fuel injection with the primary diesel injection system directly or indirectly, including by limiting supplemental injection to prevent excessive equivalence ratio, knock, misfire, high exhaust temperature, turbocharger overspeed, excessive cylinder pressure, emissions noncompliance, or catalyst overheating.

In certain embodiments, the controller calculates the supplemental-fuel quantity according to a control relationship including: a driver-demand term representative of requested torque or power; an efficiency-offset term representative of the difference between requested output and an efficient engine output; and a grade-compensation term representative of current or predicted road grade, elevation change, rolling resistance, vehicle mass, or route topology. The resulting command may be bounded by minimum and maximum injection limits and may be further corrected for ambient temperature, altitude, intake pressure, oxygen concentration, fuel temperature, supplemental-fuel pressure, and engine transient conditions.

The apparatus may further include a supplemental-fuel pump, pressure regulator, filter, shutoff valve, flow sensor, pressure sensor, temperature sensor, level sensor, and diagnostic circuit. The controller may monitor the supply circuit for leakage, low fuel level, injector malfunction, pressure deviation, or abnormal engine response and may disable supplemental fueling upon detection of a fault. A check valve or flame arresting device may be disposed between the intake passage and the supplemental-fuel reservoir to inhibit backflow or ignition propagation.

Accordingly, the apparatus provides a controlled intake-introduced oxygenated-fuel system for a diesel engine in which supplemental fueling is not merely proportional to accelerator position or engine load, but is adaptively varied according to road grade or topology and according to whether the engine output requested by the driver is above, below, or within an efficient operating range of the engine.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
